slides.headline: Sciatica or ordinary back pain?
slides.sub: Where the pain travels gives useful clues. Here's how they usually differ.

slides.title: Ordinary back pain
slides.body: It usually sits across the lower back and maybe into the buttock. It often changes with position and movement, and most episodes settle over days to weeks when you stay active.

slides.title: What sciatica usually feels like
slides.body: Pain that travels down the leg, often below the knee, sometimes with pins and needles or numbness. The leg can hurt more than the back. It comes from an irritated nerve root.

slides.title: Both usually improve
slides.body: Sciatica can be more intense and take longer, often weeks to a few months. Still, most people improve with time, movement and conservative care. Staying gently active helps in both cases.

slides.title: What helps in the meantime
slides.body: Short walks, changing position often and gentle movements you can tolerate. Avoid long stretches of bed rest. Your physio can suggest positions and exercises that ease leg symptoms.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Numbness around the groin, changes in bladder or bowel control, leg weakness that's getting worse, or symptoms in both legs. These need urgent medical attention, so seek help straight away.

slides.headline: Not sure which you've got?

caption:
Pain in your back, or pain running down your leg? The difference matters.

Ordinary back pain usually stays in the lower back and buttock and changes with position. Sciatica usually travels down the leg, often past the knee, sometimes with pins and needles or numbness, and the leg can hurt more than the back.

Both usually improve. Sciatica can take longer, but most people get better with time, movement and conservative care. Short walks and regular position changes tend to help more than bed rest.

Numbness around the groin, bladder or bowel changes or worsening leg weakness needs urgent medical attention.
